newsitem.title: USA: NYS Control Board sees less risk in NYC budget.
newsitem.headline: NYS Control Board sees less risk in NYC budget.

text.p: The New York State Financial Control Board, created in the mid-1970s to help New York City deal with its fiscal crisis, on Tuesday projected the city's 1998 budget faced $778 million of risks.

Financial sources, who declined to be identified, had said the fiscal watchdog likely would report a much smaller amount of risk than the city or the state comptrollers, in part because the board was not as gloomy about whether the city would get all the aid it wanted from the state.

Further, the board was able to take into account Albany's decision last week to extend the city's personal income tax surcharge, which should produce approximately $400 million, the sources had explained. They declined to be named.
The state comptroller has estimated that the Giuliani Administration's preliminary budget for fiscal 1998 faced as much as $2 billion of risk.

A spokesman for the Financial Control Board, Jeffrey Sommer, said that the monitor agreed with the city's projection that bigger earnings from Wall Street financial houses would help it end fiscal 1997 on June 30 with an approximately $391 million surplus, but added it felt it still faced $68 million of risk in that year.

And the Financial Control Board, much like the city and state comptrollers, took a harsh line over the outyear gaps the city faces, projecting they would add up to over $2.3 billion in fiscal 1999 and more than $3 billion in both fiscal 2000 and 2001. "At no time in the past 20 years, if ever, has the city identified as large a midyear surplus as that contained in the February modification. It should take advantage of this opportunity to begin to correct the embedded structural imbalance," it said, in prepared remarks.
